title: Richardson v. Perales (1971)
summary: Reliable examining-physician reports could constitute substantial evidence despite hearsay objections when the claimant did not use the available subpoena procedure.
notes: Blackmun wrote for a 6-3 Court; Douglas dissented joined by Black and Brennan, objecting that a claimant's benefits were denied on the basis of unsworn written reports by physicians he could not cross-examine.

sections.Parties: Perales applied for Social Security disability benefits after a work-related back injury. The Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare defended the agency’s denial and its use of written medical evidence.
sections.Material Facts: Perales underwent surgery and continued to report pain. His treating general practitioner considered him permanently disabled, while several examining specialists found only mild impairment or no objective explanation for major limitations. At two hearings Perales, his physician, and others testified. The examiner also used the written specialist reports and an independent medical adviser who reviewed the evidence without examining Perales. Perales’s lawyer cross-examined that adviser but never requested subpoenas for the report authors, whose identities and reports were available.
sections.Procedural History: The state agency denied the application and reconsideration; a hearing examiner denied benefits and the Appeals Council upheld the decision. Perales obtained judicial review under the Social Security Act. The Fifth Circuit accepted admissibility of the reports and adviser testimony but held that the evidence could not constitute substantial evidence when objected to and contradicted by live testimony. The Supreme Court reversed and remanded for the district court to evaluate the merits using all admissible material.
sections.Issue: Can examining physicians’ written reports constitute substantial evidence supporting denial of disability benefits despite hearsay objections, no actual cross-examination of their authors, and contrary live testimony? Did the medical adviser or the hearing structure defeat fundamental fairness?
sections.Holding: The reports could constitute substantial evidence under these conditions. The available subpoena mechanism, not invoked by the represented claimant, provided an opportunity for cross-examination. The medical adviser’s participation was not inherently improper. The Court expressly declined to decide whether Perales was disabled and left the substantial-evidence determination on the complete record for remand.
sections.Reasoning:
The Social Security Act allows relevant evidence that courtroom evidence rules would exclude and gives the agency procedural flexibility subject to fairness. The reports came from licensed specialists who had personally examined Perales; their consistency, medical content, and routine preparation supported reliability. The claimant knew and could inspect the adverse material and could seek subpoenas. The Court distinguished Goldberg’s termination setting and concerns about credibility and the ability to present a case. It viewed the nonexamining medical adviser as helping a lay examiner understand technical evidence, without pretending he had verified the underlying facts personally.

The Court did not resolve the APA’s general applicability because the relevant Social Security procedures were consistent with § 556(d), including relevant documentary evidence and cross-examination needed for full factual disclosure. Douglas, joined by Black and Brennan, considered live cross-examination of these doctors essential and rejected reliance on untested government-retained reports to defeat a claim. The later notes qualify an easy reading of the majority: agency regulations do not promise issuance of every requested subpoena, and reliability remains a substantive question.

topics.lrs-o-administrative-evidence: Written medical reports could be substantial evidence where the claimant had but did not use the subpoena mechanism to obtain confrontation.
topics.lrs-o-adjudication-stages: The Court assessed a staged benefits system in which the examiner developed the record rather than importing every adversarial-trial convention.
topics.lrs-o-due-process-framework: The claimant argued that reliance on unexamined written reports violated due process, and the Court measured the hearing procedure against that standard.
